# Project 5: Bayesian Regression {#sec-project-5 .unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Project at a glance

**Prerequisites:** @sec-prediction, @sec-gibbs, @sec-regression, @sec-model-comparison.
**Effort:** about 15 hours.
**Deliverable:** a reproducible report (at most 10 pages plus code).
**Skills:** specifying and fitting a Bayesian linear regression; interpreting coefficients on a transformed scale; posterior prediction; posterior predictive checks; sensitivity to priors, transformations, influential observations and missing-data handling.
:::

## Scientific question {#sec-p5-question}

How are daily ozone concentrations in New York related to solar radiation, wind speed and temperature? And what ozone level should be expected on a hot, calm, sunny summer day?

## Data {#sec-p5-data}

`datasets::airquality` contains 153 daily measurements from New York, May to September 1973. The variables are mean ozone in parts per billion (Roosevelt Island, 13:00–15:00), solar radiation in Langleys (Central Park, 08:00–12:00), average wind speed in mph (LaGuardia Airport), maximum daily temperature in °F (LaGuardia Airport), month and day. The R documentation states that the data were obtained from the New York State Department of Conservation (ozone) and the National Weather Service (meteorological data), and cites @chambers1983graphical. They are distributed with R ("Part of R", GPL).

**Missing data.** Ozone is missing on 37 days and solar radiation on 7. We use the 111 complete cases. This is valid if missingness is unrelated to the unobserved values given the predictors (missing at random, MAR), and loses information either way. Task 6 asks you to examine this assumption.

**Preprocessing.** Predictors are standardised, with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 computed on the complete cases. The response is analysed on the log scale, with the raw-scale model as a comparison.

## Model {#sec-p5-model}

$$
\log y_i\mid\beta,\sigma^2\sim\mathrm N(x_i^\top\beta,\sigma^2),\qquad \beta\mid\sigma^2\sim\mathrm N(0,\sigma^2V_0),\qquad \sigma^2\sim\mathrm{IG}(1,1),
$$
with $V_0=\mathrm{diag}(100,1,1,1)$: a vague prior for the intercept, and slopes for which a one-standard-deviation change in a predictor multiplying ozone by more than $e^{2\sigma}$ is a priori unlikely. This is the conjugate normal–inverse-gamma regression of @sec-regression, fitted with `conjugate_linear_regression()`.

## Tasks {#sec-p5-tasks}

**Task 1 (exploration).** Plot the data, and justify the log transformation and the choice of predictors.

**Task 2 (fit and interpret).** Fit the conjugate model exactly, and also with the semi-conjugate Gibbs sampler `gibbs_linear_regression()`. Interpret each coefficient as a multiplicative effect on ozone per standard deviation of the predictor, with 90% intervals.

**Task 3 (prediction).** Compute the posterior predictive distribution of ozone for a day with temperature 90 °F, wind 5 mph and solar radiation 250 Langleys. Report the predictive median and a 90% interval on the ozone scale, and distinguish predictive uncertainty from uncertainty about the mean.

**Task 4 (checking).** Carry out posterior predictive checks of the minimum, maximum and skewness of ozone, for the log-scale model and the raw-scale model. Also check the residuals for autocorrelation over days.

**Task 5 (sensitivity).** Assess sensitivity to the prior scale $V_0$ (×0.1 and ×100), to adding month as a factor, and to removing the single most extreme observation.

**Task 6 (missing data).** Compare the complete cases with the incomplete ones on the observed variables. Is MAR plausible? Outline how the Bayesian model could be extended to impute missing solar radiation.

## Starter code {#sec-p5-starter}

```{r}
#| label: p5-starter
aq <- airquality
colSums(is.na(aq))
cc <- aq[complete.cases(aq[, c("Ozone", "Solar.R", "Wind", "Temp")]), ]
std <- function(v, ref = v) (v - mean(ref)) / sd(ref)
X <- with(cc, cbind(intercept = 1, solar = std(Solar.R), wind = std(Wind), temp = std(Temp)))
y_log <- log(cc$Ozone)
dim(X)
```

## Assessment {#sec-p5-assessment}

Assessed with the [capstone rubric](capstone.qmd#sec-capstone-rubric). The emphasis is on interpretation (Tasks 2–3), checking (Task 4), and the honesty of the sensitivity and missing-data discussion (Tasks 5–6).

## Solution guide {#sec-p5-solutions}

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Tasks 1–2
```{r}
#| label: fig-p5-explore
#| fig-cap: "Ozone against temperature on the raw and log scales (complete cases). The raw scale shows increasing spread and curvature, which the log scale largely removes."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(cc$Temp, cc$Ozone, pch = 16, col = alpha_col(course_cols[1], 0.6), xlab = "temperature (°F)", ylab = "ozone (ppb)")
plot(cc$Temp, log(cc$Ozone), pch = 16, col = alpha_col(course_cols[2], 0.6), xlab = "temperature (°F)", ylab = "log ozone")
par(op)
```
```{r}
#| label: p5-fit
set.seed(501)
V0 <- diag(c(100, 1, 1, 1))
fit_log <- conjugate_linear_regression(X, y_log, V0 = V0)
d_log <- fit_log$draw(4000)
gb <- gibbs_linear_regression(X, y_log, 5000, S0 = V0)[-(1:500), ]
cbind(exact_mean = colMeans(d_log), gibbs_mean = colMeans(gb),
      mult_effect = c(NA, exp(colMeans(d_log)[2:4]), NA),
      mult_q05 = c(NA, exp(apply(d_log[, 2:4], 2, quantile, 0.05)), NA),
      mult_q95 = c(NA, exp(apply(d_log[, 2:4], 2, quantile, 0.95)), NA)) |> round(3)
```
The two fits agree closely. They use slightly different priors: the Gibbs prior on $\beta$ does not scale with $\sigma^2$. A one-standard-deviation increase in temperature (about 9 °F) multiplies expected ozone by about 1.6 (90% interval roughly 1.45–1.75), holding the other predictors fixed. Wind reduces ozone by about 20% per standard deviation (about 3.5 mph), and solar radiation increases it by about 25%. These are associations in observational data, conditional on the other predictors, and not causal effects. Note that $\exp(\mathbb E[\beta])$ is the posterior median of the multiplicative effect only approximately, and that the median of $\exp(\beta)$ equals $\exp$ of the median of $\beta$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 3
```{r}
#| label: p5-predict
x_new <- c(1, std(250, cc$Solar.R), std(5, cc$Wind), std(90, cc$Temp))
mu_new <- as.vector(d_log[, 1:4] %*% x_new)
y_new <- exp(rnorm(nrow(d_log), mu_new, sqrt(d_log[, "sigma2"])))
rbind(mean_ozone_median_scale = quantile(exp(mu_new), c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)),
      predicted_ozone = quantile(y_new, c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95))) |> round(1)
```
The posterior for the *typical* (median) ozone on such a day is fairly narrow. The predictive interval for an *individual* day is several times wider, because it includes the residual variation $\sigma^2$, which dominates. On the original scale the predictive distribution is right-skewed: report quantiles, not mean ± sd.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 4
```{r}
#| label: p5-ppc
fit_raw <- conjugate_linear_regression(X, cc$Ozone, V0 = diag(c(1e4, 1e2, 1e2, 1e2)))
d_raw <- fit_raw$draw(4000)
skew <- function(v) mean((v - mean(v))^3) / sd(v)^3
rep_stat <- function(d, f, logscale) apply(d, 1, function(r) {
  yr <- rnorm(nrow(X), X %*% r[1:4], sqrt(r[5])); f(if (logscale) exp(yr) else yr) })
set.seed(502)
stats <- list(min = min, max = max, skewness = skew)
t(sapply(stats, function(f) c(observed = f(cc$Ozone), ppp_log_model = ppc_pvalue(f(cc$Ozone), rep_stat(d_log, f, TRUE)),
                              ppp_raw_model = ppc_pvalue(f(cc$Ozone), rep_stat(d_raw, f, FALSE))))) |> round(3)
res <- y_log - X %*% colMeans(d_log)[1:4]
c(lag1_autocorrelation = acf(res, plot = FALSE)$acf[2], min_residual = min(res), which_min = cc$Ozone[which.min(res)])
```
Recall that the p-value is $\mathbb P(T^{\mathrm{rep}}\ge T^{\mathrm{obs}})$, so values near 0 or 1 indicate conflict. The raw-scale model fails clearly. Its replications contain negative ozone values, so every replicated minimum is below the observed one ($p=0$), and it cannot reproduce the right skew or the large maximum ($p\approx0$ for both). The log model reproduces the maximum and the skewness acceptably. Its one weakness is the minimum: the observed minimum of 1 ppb is smaller than almost every replicated minimum ($p\approx1$), because that single day has a large negative log residual. The lag-1 autocorrelation of residuals in day order is small, so ignoring serial dependence is a minor issue here, although daily data could in general require a time-series model (@sec-time-series).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 5
```{r}
#| label: p5-sensitivity
fit_coef <- function(X, y, V0) { f <- conjugate_linear_regression(X, y, V0 = V0); setNames(f$m, colnames(X)) }
Xm <- cbind(X, model.matrix(~ factor(Month), cc)[, -1]); colnames(Xm)[5:8] <- paste0("month", 6:9)
drop <- which.min(y_log - X %*% colMeans(d_log)[1:4])
rbind(baseline = fit_coef(X, y_log, V0),
      prior_x0.1 = fit_coef(X, y_log, V0 * 0.1),
      prior_x100 = fit_coef(X, y_log, V0 * 100),
      with_month = fit_coef(Xm, y_log, diag(c(100, rep(1, 7))))[1:4],
      drop_min_obs = fit_coef(X[-drop, ], y_log[-drop], V0)) |> round(3)
```
Making the prior 100 times wider changes nothing of substance. The narrower prior (×0.1, a prior standard deviation of about 0.16 for each slope on the log scale, given $\sigma\approx0.52$) shrinks the temperature coefficient by about 7%. "Weakly informative" depends on the scale of the problem. Adding month barely changes the slopes and mainly shifts the intercept: temperature already captures most of the seasonal variation that matters for ozone. Removing the single 1 ppb day changes the slopes by 0.03–0.05 (10–13%), so one observation has noticeable influence. This is consistent with the minimum check in Task 4, and motivates a heavier-tailed Student-$t$ error model as a robustness check.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Task 6
```{r}
#| label: p5-missing
aq$missing <- !complete.cases(aq[, c("Ozone", "Solar.R")])
aggregate(cbind(Wind, Temp) ~ missing, data = aq, FUN = mean) |> round(2)
table(month = aq$Month, missing = aq$missing)
```
On the observed predictors, incomplete and complete days have similar average wind and temperature. Missingness is concentrated in June, however, when ozone is missing on 21 of 30 days, so it is related to season, which is associated with ozone. Complete-case analysis is then valid only if, given the predictors in the model, missingness is unrelated to ozone. Including month as a predictor makes that more plausible. A Bayesian extension treats missing solar radiation as unknown parameters with a model, e.g. $\text{Solar.R}_i\sim\mathrm N(\gamma_0+\gamma_1\text{Temp}_i,\omega^2)$, sampled within the Gibbs sampler alongside $\beta$ (data augmentation, @sec-gibbs). Missing *responses* under MAR contribute nothing to the likelihood for $\beta$ and can be predicted afterwards.
:::
